note: A man found pitch near a winepress and came to ask Rav what to do with it. Rav told him to take it for himself. Seeing the man still hesitate, Rav said: go and share it with my son Hiyya, showing he was sure it was not stolen property.
why: The discussion asks whether the place where an item is found counts as a mark that lets the owner reclaim it. Rav's ruling seems to say no, but Rabbi Abba explains it otherwise: grass had grown through the pitch, so its owner had long given up on it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the great academy at Sura in Babylonia, one of the most important early Sages of the Talmud.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage who explains the reasoning behind Rav's ruling.

terms.meaning: A feature an owner can describe to prove a lost item is his. A finder must announce items that have one; items without one may often be kept.
Once an owner has given up hope of getting a lost item back, it becomes ownerless and the finder may keep it.

note: Rav borrowed gold dinars from the daughter of Rabbi Hiyya. By the time he came to repay, gold dinars had risen in value, and Rav worried that returning them would mean paying her interest. He went to Rabbi Hiyya, who told him: go and pay her back in good, full-weight dinars.
why: The Gemara is asking whether gold coins count as money or as goods compared with silver, and reads this ruling as showing Rabbi Hiyya treated gold as money. It then rejects the proof: Rav had dinars of his own elsewhere, which changes the case.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the academy at Sura in Babylonia; he had studied in the Land of Israel and was related to Rabbi Hiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the Mishna, Rav's teacher and uncle.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a Jew to pay or take any extra on a loan to another Jew, including repaying goods that have gone up in value.
A measure of volume for grain and produce. Lending a se'a of produce and getting a se'a back is forbidden, because prices may rise in between.

note: Abba Mar, the son of Rav Pappa, used to accept pans of wax from wax makers and then ask his father to lend them money. The Sages complained to Rav Pappa that his son was taking interest. Rav Pappa replied that interest of this kind is fine: the Torah forbids only interest that passes from borrower to lender, and his son was simply being paid for putting in a word.
why: Rava has just ruled that a person may take a fee for asking someone else to make a loan; this case shows the ruling in practice.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Son of Rav Pappa, who earned wax for arranging loans from his father.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, head of an academy at Naresh.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a lender to take any extra from a Jewish borrower in return for a loan.
